title: Choose the player-props page structure
question: Which composition makes it easiest to tune the score, compare leans, and understand why the ranking changed?

options.label: Matchup Board
options.thesis: Two team columns turn the game into a head-to-head prop board while one shared scoring console governs both sides.
options.viewport: Game identity and three compact weight sliders span the top; below, away and home prop columns mirror each other with cumulative-score leaders nearest the center seam.
options.risk: Team symmetry can make cross-team ranking slightly slower when one side has far more props.

options.label: Market Lanes
options.thesis: Props flow through horizontal market lanes so users compare like with like before opening the evidence behind a lean.
options.viewport: A sticky scoring strip sits under the game header; strikeouts, outs, hits, and total-bases lanes fill the page with ranked cards and visible three-factor bars.
options.risk: A user seeking one player must scan across several lanes unless search and player filters are prominent.

options.label: Top Lean First
options.thesis: The strongest cumulative lean becomes the focal analysis, followed by a dense ranked board of every alternative.
options.viewport: The game header and weights lead into one large best-lean module with a three-part score decomposition; the remaining props continue below as a compact sortable table.
options.risk: The focal recommendation may feel overly authoritative unless uncertainty and score proximity are explicit.
